facts.text: Zeiram was director Keita Amemiya's second film, but his first released in theaters. His earlier Mirai Ninja (1988) went straight to video.
Murata, the bar buddy, was voiced in the English dub by Steve Kramer, who also wrote the dub's script for Streamline Pictures.
Before directing, Keita Amemiya was a character designer on TV's Choujin Sentai Jetman and later Kyoryu Sentai Zyuranger, and he went on to direct Kamen Rider ZO.
Yukijiro Hotaru (Kamiya) coached newcomer Yuko Moriyama on acting, and he hunched over on set so that Moriyama's Iria would look bigger and more imposing next to him.
Zeiram began life as a project called "HP9999," with a video-game theme and a story about a robot and a young man. Director Keita Amemiya then created Iria because he wanted a heroine.
Yuko Moriyama (Iria) was mostly known for TV work and a contact-lens commercial. She hesitated to take the part because she had no action experience.
Teppei actor Kunihiro Ida and Zeiram suit actor Mizuho Yoshida were both Keita Amemiya regulars. Ida appeared in the director's earlier Mirai Ninja, which was also Yoshida's first role.
The Zone town was shot in real Mikasa, Hokkaido, Japan, and the film names it onscreen as the "zero point."
Zeiram cost about 30 million yen, roughly $200,000, less than director Keita Amemiya's earlier Mirai Ninja. That's about what one episode of his later TV series Garo cost.
Zeiram's designer was Keita Amemiya himself. Per Asian Movie Pulse, his suit is detailed yet still lets actor Mizuho Yoshida move, and Yoshida's height gives it presence.
Suit actor Mizuho Yoshida (Zeiram) later played Godzilla in Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001) and the Legion Queen in Gamera 2.
Yuko Moriyama said Iria's armor was so bulky it bruised her and took about a month to get used to. It was also so squeaky that you could always hear her coming.
Director Keita Amemiya recalls a 37-hour shoot with no sleep or rest during Zeiram. He says location limits also forced script changes.
A motorcycle stunt was shot in a plane hangar at Haneda Airport. Director Keita Amemiya had never filmed such a stunt, and the rider's wire snapped, which could have badly hurt the Zeiram suit actor.
Special effects director Hajime Matsumoto mixed suitmation, stop-motion, puppetry, animatronics, miniatures, gore and a little CGI, all on a budget well below that year's Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.
The smoke in the attack by the small Lilliput monster was made with oil, shot at 2 a.m. It coated the neighbors' laundry, and director Keita Amemiya later apologized to them.
The Fangoria review of the US release said it wanted to "reach into the picture tube and slap" the two electricians. It still called the film "loads of hi-tech fun."
The film's tentacle attack was worked with wires. The prop was too short, so the crew used camera tricks to make it look longer. It was among the last scenes shot.
LA Weekly said Zeiram's effects were "so insidious they're the stuff of nightmares and so cheesy they're the stuff of fondue." It compared the film to Blade Runner, Alien and The Thing.
The Bedlam Files argued that Zeiram's computer-run interdimensional battleground anticipated The Matrix (1999), and noted its tough female lead was rare in early-90s Hollywood.
The English dub was made by Streamline Pictures, with Carl Macek directing the voices. Macek was the man behind Robotech, and the film was released in the US as "Zeram" in 1994.
A reviewer at The Stop Button compared Zeiram to the low-budget Trancers. The site noted the Zone is a copy of a city with no extras, and tight shots suggest cramped, adjoining sets.
Zeiram spawned a 1994 sequel, Zeiram 2, and a six-episode anime prequel, Iria: Zeiram the Animation. It also got a PlayStation game, ZeiramZone.
Asian Movie Pulse noted that director Keita Amemiya's stated dislike of sexism and hierarchy shows in the film's role reversals: the bounty hunter Iria rescues the two bumbling male electricians.
Zeiram's skeleton form was made by combining stop-motion animation with puppetry, one of several old-school effects techniques director Keita Amemiya's crew used.
Jonathan Clements wrote that Yuko Moriyama's screen presence as Iria was a major factor in the film's appeal and in the franchise that followed.
Yukijiro Hotaru (Kamiya) later played Gonza Kurahashi in the Garo TV franchise. Garo was created by Zeiram director Keita Amemiya.
Zeiram was a fixture of film-festival Midnight Madness programs, according to The Bedlam Files, and Fox Lorber's US VHS box called it "a breakthrough in futuristic space adventure."
The film got a US theatrical life too: it screened at Cambridge's Brattle Theatre in March 1994 and premiered in New York at the Westbury Theater that April.
Zeiram 2 won a Seiun Award. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction's reviewer questioned it, blaming forgiving Media-category voters during a wave of Hollywood effects movies like Jurassic Park.
